Latent Sparse Attention: Towards Subquadratic
Ultra-Long Context Attention

 

Ales Kubicek * 1  Andrea Caciolai * 1  Liangzu Peng * 1  Sukrit Sumant 1  Benjamin Hoover 1  Fraser Greenlee 1  Ruairidh M. Battleday 1  Radim Urban 2  Torsten Hoefler 2  James C.R. Whittington † 1 

††footnotetext: *Core contributors. † Senior author. 1Prefrontal AI, London, United Kingdom 2ETH Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland. Correspondence to: Ales Kubicek <ales@prefrontal.ai>, James C.R. Whittington <james@prefrontal.ai>.
Preprint.
Abstract

Agentic workflows are increasingly shifting towards long-horizon tasks, such as open-ended scientific work, where models benefit from long context windows. However, at ultra-long context (above 1M tokens), full attention is prohibitively expensive. A promising approach is sparse attention, in which a dedicated indexer selects a subset of keys for the attention. Yet current methods of indexing either still have quadratic cost in context size or lose accuracy at ultra-long context scale. We address this with Latent Sparse Attention (LSA), an efficient attention method that maintains accuracy at ultra-long context. In LSA, keys are hierarchically clustered in a learned latent space, and queries score the hierarchy of clusters instead of scoring every key, making prefill, decode and training faster at long context. We propose two variants, Distilled-LSA (D-LSA), which can be applied to pre-trained models via distillation, and Native-LSA (N-LSA), which is trained natively on the next-token loss alone. On GLM-5.3-Flash (Qwen-3.8-27B) at 10M tokens, D-LSA speeds up one attention layer by 22.7×22.7\times (72.4×72.4\times) in prefill and 4.6×4.6\times (42.5×42.5\times) in decode over its original sparse attention (full attention), while keeping similar accuracy across a variety of tasks. N-LSA matches the accuracy of full attention with a training speedup of 1.6×1.6\times per layer at 128k tokens. LSA offers practical and efficient attention for models to benefit from ultra-long context.

1 Introduction

Large language models have moved from answering single requests to agentic workflows in long-horizon tasks, such as software engineering and open-ended scientific research (Jimenez et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2026). These tasks keep growing in length (Kwa et al., 2025), and models with longer context windows tend to score higher on them (Zhu et al., 2026). In line with this trend, recent models extend their context windows to 1M tokens and beyond (Gemini Team, 2024; MiniMax, 2025; DeepSeek-AI, 2026a; Qwen Team, 2026a).

At this context size, attention dominates the cost, as its work grows with context (Vaswani et al., 2017; Dao et al., 2022). An established technique to reduce such costs is sparse attention (Hoefler et al., 2021), in which each query attends to only a subset of the keys, chosen by a fixed pattern (Child et al., 2019; Beltagy et al., 2020; Zaheer et al., 2020), by their content (Kitaev et al., 2020; Roy et al., 2021), or by a dedicated indexer (Yuan et al., 2025; DeepSeek-AI, 2025). Recent frontier models are increasingly adopting sparse attention, in which keys are selected using a dedicated indexer (DeepSeek-AI, 2025; Qwen Team, 2026a).

However, current indexers still score every preceding key, or block of keys, for each query. This remains expensive (quadratic in prefill, linear in decode), and becomes a bottleneck at long context (Zan et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026). For example, at 10M tokens, 98% of the prefill time of a sparse attention layer is spent on indexing (Figure 2). The cost of sparse attention at ultra-long context is therefore dominated by the cost of finding the keys.

To address this, we introduce Latent Sparse Attention (LSA), which clusters keys in a learned latent space and lets each query search the clusters instead of scoring every key. This can be done using only one level of clustering (Flat), or with a hierarchy of clusters (Tree), which makes the prefill subquadratic. Furthermore, we propose two trainable designs: D-LSA, which adds LSA to pre-trained models and only trains small projection matrices per layer (contribution #1), and N-LSA, which trains LSA natively with the Next-Token Prediction (NTP) loss alone (contribution #2). We evaluate state-of-the-art models (Qwen-3.8-27B and GLM-5.3-Flash) beyond their advertised context, up to 10M tokens (contribution #3), on RULER (Hsieh et al., 2024), which is an established long-context benchmark, and PaperTrail, which we developed to test long-context scientific understanding by finding and connecting facts across unseen scientific papers (contribution #4). Finally, we integrate LSA into SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024)11 1  github.com/Prefrontal-AI/sglang with context parallelism, provide GPU kernels for H200 and B300, and release the code22 2  github.com/Prefrontal-AI/latent-sparse-attention with all training and inference details (contribution #5). Figure 1 outlines our contributions.

2 Sparse Attention

In full attention, every query attends to every preceding key. Prefilling a context of TT tokens therefore costs 𝒪⁡(T2)\mathcal{O}(T^{2}), and decoding one token costs 𝒪⁡(T)\mathcal{O}(T). In sparse attention, the work is split between an indexer and the attention. For each query, the indexer selects which keys the attention attends to33 3 In this view, full attention corresponds to an indexer that returns the indices of all preceding keys.. With a fixed budget of kk keys, the attention then costs 𝒪⁡(T​k)\mathcal{O}(Tk) to prefill and 𝒪⁡(k)\mathcal{O}(k) per decoded token. If the indexer selects the most relevant keys, this is sufficient to stay close to the accuracy of full attention (Appendix A).

However, the indexer has a cost. Since it must score all preceding keys, it typically remains 𝒪⁡(T2)\mathcal{O}(T^{2}) in prefill and 𝒪⁡(T)\mathcal{O}(T) in decode, though with reduced constant factors. This makes ultra-long context still prohibitively expensive. For example, at 10M tokens the indexer takes 98% of the prefill time of traditional sparse attention (Figure 2), and a ‘free’ indexer would make sparse attention a further 58×58\times faster in prefill and 8.9×8.9\times in decode.

2.1 Design Choices

Sparse attention methods can be categorised by their indexer designs and how they are trained.

Token Sparse Attention. For each query, a lightweight indexer (fewer heads, smaller dimension, lower precision) scores every preceding key and selects which to attend to.

Block Sparse Attention. Consecutive keys are grouped into blocks, and each query scores blocks instead of every key. All keys of the selected blocks are sent to the attention.

Semantic Sparse Attention. Keys are clustered by similarity rather than position, and each query scores one centroid per cluster. All keys of the selected clusters are sent to the attention.

For the last two categories, a query can search the groups in three ways. Flat search scores every group directly, which is 𝒪⁡(T)\mathcal{O}(T) work per query. Fixed search adds a shallow hierarchy and refines from coarse to fine groups, which is also 𝒪⁡(T)\mathcal{O}(T) per query. Tree search descends a deeper hierarchy and expands only the groups it keeps at each level, which is 𝒪⁡(log⁡T)\mathcal{O}(\log T) per query.

An indexer can be training-free, distilled from a pre-trained model, or trained natively on the NTP loss alone.

2.2 Related Work

Table 1 provides an overview of the existing work on sparse attention, as categorised above. We focus on methods that keep the whole KV cache and select keys per query, unlike fixed sparse patterns (Child et al., 2019; Beltagy et al., 2020; Zaheer et al., 2020) and KV cache eviction techniques (Zhang et al., 2023b; Li et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2024b).

Among distillation methods, DSA (DeepSeek-AI, 2025) and MiniMax SA (Lai et al., 2026) first distil the indexer and then continue training the full model under sparse attention. Alternatively, SeerAttention (Gao et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2026) distils a gate over pooled blocks and HashAttention (Desai et al., 2025) learns binary codes of queries and keys, both with the model frozen. As the context grows, the indexer itself becomes the bottleneck (Xu et al., 2026; Zan et al., 2026; Bai et al., 2026). To reduce its cost, CSA (DeepSeek-AI, 2026a), QSA (Qwen Team, 2026a), and GLM-5.3-Flash SA (Z.ai, 2026) compress every four keys into one before scoring them. HISA (Xu et al., 2026) and LongCat LSA (Zan et al., 2026) score blocks first and then only the keys inside the selected blocks. IndexCache (Bai et al., 2026), LongCat LSA and DeepSeek-V4.1 (DeepSeek-AI, 2026b) reuse the selection of one layer in the following layers. Each improvement divides the cost of the indexer by a constant, and its work per query therefore still grows linearly with the context.

NSA (Yuan et al., 2025) and MoBA (Lu et al., 2025) instead pre-train the model with sparse attention from scratch, such that the indexer learns from the NTP loss alone. NSA scores each block by a learned compressed key, and MoBA by the mean of its keys. InfLLM-V2 (Zhao et al., 2026) and SSA (Mao et al., 2026a) bring such block selection to existing dense models by fine-tuning. HSA (Hu et al., 2025; Leng et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026a) and HSA-UltraLong (Hu et al., 2026b) also weight the output of each block by its score, such that the loss trains the scores directly. All of these methods still scan every block. PISA (Tang et al., 2026) replaces this scan with a tree, but evaluates accuracy only at small scale (up to 16k tokens).

At the other end, Quest (Tang et al., 2024), InfLLM (Xiao et al., 2024a) and MInference (Jiang et al., 2024) select blocks based on simple summaries of their keys without any training. HiP (Lee et al., 2025a) searches the blocks with a tree, and its successor InfiniteHiP (Lee et al., 2025b) with three fixed stages. BLASST (Yuan et al., 2026) instead skips blocks directly inside the attention kernel, without a dedicated indexer. Most of these methods summarise blocks of consecutive keys, which may hide a single relevant key (Xiao et al., 2024a; Hu et al., 2026a).

Closest to LSA are methods that organise the keys by semantic content rather than by position. A few early works train at short context, with Reformer (Kitaev et al., 2020) hashing keys into buckets, Routing Transformer (Roy et al., 2021) learning k-means centroids, and Treeformer (Madaan et al., 2023) routing each query down a learned tree. Most other works here only operate at inference time: ClusterKV (Liu et al., 2025b) and RetroInfer (Chen et al., 2026) cluster the keys during prefill and score every centroid at decode (flat search), Squeezed Attention (Hooper et al., 2025b), Multipole Attention (Hooper et al., 2025a) and LycheeCluster (Li et al., 2026) search two levels (fixed search), and IceCache (Mao et al., 2026b) descends a tree of keys (tree search), while RetrievalAttention (Liu et al., 2025a) links the keys in a nearest-neighbour graph. All of these inference methods are training-free, only Squeezed Attention speeds up prefill, and only partially, and none are evaluated at ultra-long context (above 1M tokens).

3 Latent Sparse Attention (LSA)

LSA is a sparse attention layer for ultra-long context. It clusters keys by content, in a space that is learned: through index projections in D-LSA, and through the attention’s own keys in N-LSA. LSA can replace the attention of a pre-trained layer by distillation (D-LSA) or be trained natively with the model (N-LSA).

In both settings, the indices for the attention are selected from the keys and queries by the same process. We first describe this process, numbered as in Figure 3, which consists of semantic clustering of the index keys kj(idx)k_{j}^{(\mathrm{idx})}, and the search with the index queries qi(idx)q_{i}^{(\mathrm{idx})} so that each query selects its keys. We then describe the specifics of D-LSA and N-LSA.

3.1 Semantic Clustering

Key normalisation. Each index key kj(idx)k_{j}^{(\mathrm{idx})} is first L2 normalised: kj(idx)←kj(idx)∥kj(idx)∥k_{j}^{(\mathrm{idx})}\leftarrow\frac{k_{j}^{(\mathrm{idx})}}{\lVert k_{j}^{(\mathrm{idx})}\rVert}

Pooling. Consecutive keys are then compressed, as in CSA (DeepSeek-AI, 2026a), QSA (Qwen Team, 2026a) and GLM-5.3-Flash SA (Z.ai, 2026), to improve computational efficiency. Here, every npooln_{\mathrm{pool}} consecutive index keys are summed into one pool key kpool(idx)k_{\mathrm{pool}}^{(\mathrm{idx})}, so that clustering runs over T/npoolT/n_{\mathrm{pool}} pool keys rather than TT keys.

Clustering. Keys are clustered in cluster blocks of nclustern_{\mathrm{cluster}} consecutive keys. Once a cluster block contains all its keys, its pool keys are clustered bottom up with Ward’s method (Ward, 1963) into mm buckets (Algorithm 1 in Appendix B). Each pool key starts as a bucket of its own, and each bucket keeps the sum of its keys, whose normalisation is its centroid cbc_{b}. In every round, all pairs of buckets that are each other’s cheapest merge are merged in parallel. The cost of a merge is how much it increases the keys’ total squared distance from their centroid (Ward’s criterion). Merging stops once there are m=ncluster/n¯bm=n_{\mathrm{cluster}}/\bar{n}_{b} buckets, where n¯b\bar{n}_{b} is the average number of keys per bucket, such that every cluster block holds the same number of buckets. A merge is skipped if the merged bucket would hold more than nbmaxn_{b}^{\mathrm{max}} keys.

Bucket cache. The bucket cache Bcache(idx)B_{\mathrm{cache}}^{(\mathrm{idx})} stores the centroid cbc_{b} of every bucket and an index table of the positions of its keys. This is so later selected buckets can ‘expand’ into their key indices. With one centroid per n¯b\bar{n}_{b} keys, it corresponds to a small fraction of the KV cache.

Once a cluster block is clustered, its buckets never change. In the Tree variant, this clustering process is repeated to group the buckets into multiple levels of a hierarchy.

3.2 Semantic Search

We now describe how the top-kk key indices are extracted for each query, and then submitted to attention. We first describe the process for Flat, in which there is only one level of buckets, and then discuss Tree.

Query normalisation. Each index query qi(idx)q_{i}^{(\mathrm{idx})} is first L2 normalised: qi(idx)←qi(idx)∥qi(idx)∥q_{i}^{(\mathrm{idx})}\leftarrow\frac{q_{i}^{(\mathrm{idx})}}{\lVert q_{i}^{(\mathrm{idx})}\rVert}

Scoring. The index query scores the unit-norm centroid of every bucket in the cluster blocks before its own via si,b=cb⋅qi(idx)s_{i,b}=c_{b}\cdot q_{i}^{(\mathrm{idx})}, which compares buckets of any size on one scale, and selects the top-pp buckets. Its own cluster block is not clustered yet, and its keys are covered by the window instead.

Expansion. The selected pp buckets are expanded into their keys, best first, until kk ‘long-range’ keys are selected. As every bucket holds at least npooln_{\mathrm{pool}} keys, pp is chosen such that p⋅npool≥kp\cdot n_{\mathrm{pool}}\geq k, and so expansion always fills kk keys.

Besides the kk long-range keys, every query attends to nsinkn_{\mathrm{sink}} sink keys (Xiao et al., 2024b) and the nwn_{w} most recent keys (window). A key of a selected bucket that falls in the sink or the window is already attended to, and the expansion moves on to the next key instead. We set the window to one cluster block, nw=nclustern_{w}=n_{\mathrm{cluster}}, so that the window covers every key not yet clustered. This gives each query ii a set JiJ_{i} of at most nsink+k+nwn_{\mathrm{sink}}+k+n_{w} key indices.

Attention. Attention is then computed only over the keys indexed by JiJ_{i}. A single JiJ_{i} is shared across all query heads.

Tree search arranges the buckets into a hierarchy (Figure 3, right). Level 0 holds the buckets, and each higher level ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1 holds buckets we term ‘node buckets’, each made of nb,ℓn_{b,\ell} buckets of the level below, with a centroid over all the keys it contains. As at level 0, buckets are merged one cluster block at a time. Buckets that are not merged yet are defined as open. Once a level holds ncluster,ℓn_{\mathrm{cluster},\ell} open buckets, they are merged into node buckets as in Algorithm 1.

Beam search is used to select the buckets through the hierarchy (Algorithm 2 in Appendix B). On each level, the query is scored against the centroids of the candidate node buckets, and the best pℓp_{\ell} are kept. The candidates on the level below are the children of the kept node buckets and the open buckets of that level. At level 0, the top-pp buckets are selected, as in the flat search. With a constant beam per level, a query scores 𝒪⁡(log⁡T)\mathcal{O}(\log T) centroids, which makes the prefill of the indexer subquadratic, 𝒪⁡(T​log⁡T)\mathcal{O}(T\log T), where the flat search is quadratic.

3.3 D-LSA

D-LSA (Figure 3) follows the process outlined above, but since it distils from a pre-trained model which already has key and query projections (kj(attn)k_{j}^{(\mathrm{attn})} and qi(attn)q_{i}^{(\mathrm{attn})}), we additionally learn separate key and query projections for LSA. In particular, each key kj(attn)k_{j}^{(\mathrm{attn})} and query qi(attn)q_{i}^{(\mathrm{attn})} is projected to a smaller dimension d(idx)d^{(\mathrm{idx})} to keep the scoring, clustering, and bucket cache cheap:

kj(idx)\displaystyle k_{j}^{(\mathrm{idx})} =kj(attn)​WK(idx)\displaystyle=k_{j}^{(\mathrm{attn})}W_{K}^{(\mathrm{idx})} (1)
qi(idx)\displaystyle q_{i}^{(\mathrm{idx})} =∑hqi,h(attn)​WQ(idx)\displaystyle=\sum_{h}q_{i,h}^{(\mathrm{attn})}W_{Q}^{(\mathrm{idx})}

The query heads are summed such that one index query serves every head, which yields the single index list JiJ_{i} per query. On Qwen-3.8-27B, whose keys and queries carry RoPE (Su et al., 2024) on a quarter of their dimensions, the projections read only the RoPE-free part. These keys and queries then go into the normalisation process as before. Trainable projections can also be replaced by the leading d(idx)d^{(\mathrm{idx})} principal directions of the keys in the layer, which project both keys and queries into one index space with no training. We call this variant D-LSA (Training-Free).

The base model’s attention is otherwise unchanged: its own queries attend only to the keys and values indexed by JiJ_{i}.

Distillation. D-LSA adds LSA to a pre-trained model by a short distillation that trains only WQ,K(idx)W_{Q,K}^{(\mathrm{idx})} and a temperature τ\tau per layer, with the base model frozen. This mirrors the dense warm-up of DSA (DeepSeek-AI, 2025), which also trains only the indexer against the head-aggregated attention of the frozen model. The distillation scores every key directly, without clustering. For a query ii of a layer, let ℛi\mathcal{R}_{i} be the keys it can select (all preceding keys outside the sink and the window). The target AiA_{i} is the attention of that frozen layer over ℛi\mathcal{R}_{i}, the softmax of each head’s logits over ℛi\mathcal{R}_{i} averaged over its nhn_{h} heads of dimension dhd_{h}, and A^i\hat{A}_{i} is the softmax of the D-LSA scores over the same keys. The distillation minimises the forward KL divergence between the two:

ℒi\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{i} =KL(Ai∥A^i)\displaystyle=\mathrm{KL}\big(A_{i}\,\|\,\hat{A}_{i}\big) (2)
Ai,j\displaystyle A_{i,j} =1nh​∑hsoftmaxj∈ℛi​(qi,h(attn)⋅kj(attn)/dh)\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{n_{h}}\textstyle\sum_{h}\mathrm{softmax}_{j\in\mathcal{R}_{i}}\big(q_{i,h}^{(\mathrm{attn})}\cdot k_{j}^{(\mathrm{attn})}/\sqrt{d_{h}}\big)
A^i,j\displaystyle\hat{A}_{i,j} =softmaxj∈ℛi​(qi(idx)⋅kj(idx)/τ)\displaystyle=\mathrm{softmax}_{j\in\mathcal{R}_{i}}\big(q_{i}^{(\mathrm{idx})}\cdot k_{j}^{(\mathrm{idx})}/\tau\big)

The temperature τ\tau sharpens the softmax of the D-LSA scores to match the peaked attention of the model, and is used only in this loss. Both projections are initialised with these principal directions.

Kernels. We write GPU kernels for the clustering, scoring, selection and expansion of the indexer, in CuTe DSL for H200 and B300, with a Triton version of each, which runs on any GPU. For the attention, we reuse existing attention kernels, such as FlashAttention-3 (Shah et al., 2024), which read the index list JiJ_{i} as a page table.

Parallelism. We integrate LSA into SGLang with support for tensor, expert, and pipeline parallelism, and for context parallelism in both prefill and decode. Context parallelism splits the KV cache across ranks by token, but LSA replicates its bucket cache on every rank. Every rank thus builds the same index and selects the same index list. The ranks only exchange the index keys of the newest tokens. This design choice trades memory for communication. At 10M tokens on GLM-5.3-Flash with context parallelism over 8 GPUs, each rank holds a 1.25 GiB share of the 10 GiB KV cache of a layer and the full 246 MiB bucket cache.

We provide further details on kernels in Appendix F.1 and on parallelism in Appendix F.2.

3.4 N-LSA

N-LSA (Figure 4) trains LSA natively with the model, using only the NTP loss. As the model learns with the selection from the start, we cluster the keys of the attention itself, without dedicated index projections. We use a single key-value head, such that one key per token serves every query head, and score each bucket by the best similarity any query head gives its centroid:

si,b=maxh⁡q^i,h⋅cbs_{i,b}=\max_{h}\hat{q}_{i,h}\cdot c_{b} (3)

where q^i,h\hat{q}_{i,h} is the normalised query of head hh. We stop the gradient through the selection, and the NTP loss trains the attention projections only through the keys each query attends to, the selected keys plus the sink and the window. N-LSA therefore adds no parameters to the model and needs no teacher, no index projections and no auxiliary loss.

The attention layers of N-LSA use no positional encoding, as is becoming more common in hybrid models, and RoPE could be supported by clustering only the RoPE-free part of the keys, as D-LSA does on Qwen-3.8-27B.

4 Evaluation

In this section, we describe the models, the methods we compare, and their settings. Then, we evaluate the accuracy of D-LSA up to 10M tokens, and its performance per attention layer and end to end. Finally, we show that N-LSA can be trained natively at an accuracy close to full attention.

4.1 Setup

Models. D-LSA aims to keep the accuracy of a model while making its attention significantly cheaper. We compare each model with D-LSA against its baseline attention, in accuracy and in performance. We demonstrate D-LSA on both a model with full attention (Qwen-3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026b; Qwen Team, 2026c)) and one with sparse attention (GLM-5.3-Flash (Z.ai, 2026)). On Qwen-3.8-27B, we also replace the attention with block sparse attention, inspired by QSA (Qwen Team, 2026a), as a second sparse baseline. We also compare flat to tree search where possible.

Methods. We compare the following methods:

  • •

    Full Attention: every query attends to every preceding key, the baseline attention of Qwen-3.8-27B.

  • •

    Block Sparse Attention (Flat): sparse attention whose indexer scores every block of four consecutive keys, as in QSA (Qwen Team, 2026a) and GLM-5.3-Flash (Z.ai, 2026).

  • •

    Block Sparse Attention (Tree): sparse attention whose indexer searches a tree over blocks of the keys of the attention itself, as in HiP (Lee et al., 2025a) and PISA (Tang et al., 2026). To represent these methods, we search a tree over blocks of keys directly on the KV cache, without training, which uses the full keys and favours accuracy over performance. We use blocks of eight keys, the most accurate of the sizes we compare (Appendix E.6).

  • •

    D-LSA (Flat) and  D-LSA (Tree): D-LSA with a flat search over every bucket centroid and with a tree search over the hierarchy of buckets. In decode, each request processes one token per step, and the tree search runs its levels one after another, which pays off only when many requests decode together. As we evaluate one request at a time, D-LSA (Tree) decodes with the flat search (Appendix F.1).

  • •

    D-LSA (Training-Free): D-LSA (Flat) with the principal directions of the keys as both projections instead of trained ones.

Every trained indexer we compare is distilled in the same way to ensure fairness.

Design parameters. Table 2 lists the parameters of every method per model. For D-LSA, we found that a budget of k=4096k=4096 long-range keys holds accuracy past 1M tokens better than smaller budgets, and these extra keys cost little next to the scan of the indexer they replace. On GLM-5.3-Flash, D-LSA (Flat) selects k=2048k=2048 long-range keys for queries before position 1M and k=4096k=4096 beyond. We found that the smaller budget keeps accuracy below 1M tokens while making the attention faster. Tuning the budget further, for example per layer or per request, is left to future work. A small index space of d(idx)=64d^{(\mathrm{idx})}=64 dimensions keeps the scoring and the clustering cheap, and we found wider spaces to add little accuracy.

Indexer distillation. We train on 352M tokens of documents of 16k to 1M tokens from seven domains, for 48k steps, each on 128 queries sampled from one document, with a learning rate of 3⋅10−43\cdot 10^{-4}. This is a fraction of the 2.1B tokens of the dense warm-up of DSA. In Equation 2, the target AiA_{i} keeps only the 2,048 keys with the most attention weight per query, renormalised over them, while A^i\hat{A}_{i} still spans all of ℛi\mathcal{R}_{i}, and τ\tau is calibrated per layer before the first step. Unlike DSA, we do not follow the distillation by training the whole model under sparse attention (sparse training), a step D-LSA also supports but we omit here due to its cost. We provide further details about the composition and construction of the dataset in Appendix C.

Benchmarks. We evaluate accuracy in three categories, each with a representative set of benchmarks. For knowledge, we use MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024) (a stratified sample of 2,000 questions) and GPQA-Diamond (Rein et al., 2024). For reasoning, we use AIME25 (four repeats) and MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2024) (100 problems). For long context, we use LongBench v2 (Bai et al., 2025) (60 questions) and the 13 tasks of RULER (Hsieh et al., 2024) from 4k to 10M tokens (100 prompts per task up to 1M and 20 beyond). Evaluating each benchmark in full at ultra-long context is prohibitively expensive, and we therefore use the subsets given in parentheses.

PaperTrail. To better understand model capabilities in a less synthetic ultra-long context setting, we extend RULER with a set of new tasks called PaperTrail. The tasks are constructed by embedding a trail of fabricated facts in a large collection of scientific papers. All papers are recent, almost all published after the release date of the models, such that no model could have seen them in training. A question can only be answered by finding the facts of its trail and connecting them, as in a literature search. Samples are built in three domains: exoplanets, long-context machine learning and quantum error correction. The questions come in three tiers of increasing difficulty, where tier 1 recalls a fact from one paper, tier 2 links facts across two papers and tier 3 traces a trail across three or more. We provide further details about the construction of PaperTrail in Appendix D.

Model sampling. We configure each model’s sampling as recommended by its model card with generation up to 163,840 tokens (Appendix E). Qwen-3.8-27B reaches 10M tokens with YaRN (Peng et al., 2024) at factor 40 (42 for PaperTrail at 10M), while GLM-5.3-Flash needs no extension as it has no explicit positional encoding.

Hardware and serving. We serve all models in SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024) on H200 and B300 GPUs. To show that D-LSA can be integrated with the main parallelism strategies, we evaluate it with tensor parallelism (TP8) and with context parallelism in both prefill and decode (CP8). We show more details in Appendix F.2. All accuracy measurements use context parallelism wherever the KV cache of a request outgrows the memory of a single GPU.

4.2 Accuracy

Figure 5 shows that on knowledge, reasoning and long-context tasks, D-LSA stays close to the accuracy of baseline Full Attention on Qwen-3.8-27B and of baseline sparse attention on GLM-5.3-Flash. PaperTrail further shows how well the models find and connect facts across large collections of scientific papers.

Knowledge and reasoning. On knowledge, reasoning and LongBench v2, D-LSA stays within the 95% confidence interval of both baselines, even with reasoning growing to tens of thousands of tokens (Appendix E). We further show that D-LSA does not measurably affect the length of the reasoning.

Long context. On Qwen-3.8-27B, D-LSA (Flat) stays within 5 points of baseline Full Attention up to 1M tokens and exceeds it at 10M tokens, at 63.9 against 59.9 on RULER and 29.1 against 19.8 on PaperTrail. It also stays above Block Sparse Attention (Flat) on RULER from 128k tokens on, in a fair comparison, as both indexers are distilled the same way.

On GLM-5.3-Flash, D-LSA (Flat) stays within 3 points of baseline sparse attention up to 1M tokens, trails it by up to 8 points at 2M to 5M tokens, and is within 4 points on RULER at 10M tokens. This comparison favours the baseline, which was trained together with the model, while D-LSA (Flat) is distilled from attention that is already sparse (with no finetuning of the base model itself). On both models, MultiKey 2, MultiKey 3 and CWE fall the most for every method, the baselines included. We break down RULER by task and PaperTrail by tier in Appendix E.

Design comparison. D-LSA (Tree) follows D-LSA (Flat) on Qwen-3.8-27B, but loses accuracy past 1M tokens on GLM-5.3-Flash, at 55.8 against 66.8 on RULER at 10M tokens. Block Sparse Attention (Tree) falls behind from 512k tokens, to about 63 on RULER at 1M tokens on both models, against 78 and 88 for D-LSA (Tree), and we therefore do not evaluate it beyond 1M tokens. Large blocks fall earlier (Appendix E.6). D-LSA (Training-Free), without any training, stays close to D-LSA (Flat) on Qwen-3.8-27B, but trails it on GLM-5.3-Flash.

D-LSA follows the accuracy of the baselines, showing that our semantic clustering can preserve accuracy up to 10M tokens. However, we do observe a steep drop in accuracy beyond 512k tokens for Block Sparse Attention (Tree).

4.3 Performance

Next, we evaluate the performance of D-LSA. We first measure a single attention layer and then the whole model in production serving.

Methodology. For one layer, we time the whole attention module, including its projections, the indexer and the attention, on a single GPU. In prefill, we time the last chunk of 32,768 queries before the given context. In decode, we time one step of one request with CUDA graph enabled (clustering is amortised across the steps). For the whole model, we serve each method in SGLang with prefill chunks of 32,768 tokens, and measure the time to first token (TTFT) and the time per output token (TPOT) of one request at a time, the median of three requests of 256 output tokens.

Figure 6 shows that the prefill speedup of D-LSA grows with the context. On GLM-5.3-Flash, it rises from 3.5×\times at 1M to 22.7×\times at 10M tokens over baseline sparse attention, and on Qwen-3.8-27B to 72.4×\times at 10M tokens over baseline Full Attention. Below 1M tokens, the gain is smaller, at 2.1×\times at 512k tokens, as the scan of every block is still cheap. Extrapolated beyond 10M tokens, the prefill of D-LSA (Tree) grows subquadratically and overtakes the flat search, and at 100M tokens it is predicted to be more than 90×\times faster than baseline sparse attention.

Decode follows the same trend, with a speedup up to 4.6×\times over baseline sparse attention and 42.5×\times over baseline Full Attention at 10M tokens, with D-LSA (Tree) decoding with the flat search. On B300, D-LSA reaches 12.5×\times and 42.9×\times in prefill and 5.2×\times and 18.4×\times in decode at 10M tokens.

D-LSA also requires less memory for its indexer. Baseline sparse attention caches an index key for every block of four keys, while D-LSA caches one centroid in its smaller index space for every bucket of about eight keys, together with the id of each key. At 10M tokens, the index of D-LSA (Flat) takes 246 MiB per layer against 331 MiB in GLM-5.3-Flash and 642 MiB in QSA. Larger buckets would shrink the index of D-LSA further.

End-to-end. Table 3 shows that the speedup of one layer carries over to the whole model at ultra-long context. On GLM-5.3-Flash, D-LSA (Flat) is on par with baseline sparse attention up to 1M tokens with CP8 and already 1.5×\times faster to first token at 1M with TP8, and at 10M tokens reduces the TTFT by 2.2×\times and the TPOT by 2.1×\times with CP8, and by 5.8×\times and 1.9×\times with TP8. On Qwen-3.8-27B, it reduces them by 9.2×\times and 2.9×\times at 10M tokens against baseline Full Attention. On B300, D-LSA (Flat) reduces the TTFT and the TPOT at 10M tokens by 1.6×\times and 2.2×\times with CP8 and by 4.8×\times and 2.6×\times with TP8 on GLM-5.3-Flash, and by 5.7×\times and 1.5×\times on Qwen-3.8-27B. The speedup of the whole model is expected to be smaller than that of one layer, as only the global attention layers become faster, while the other layers keep their cost.

4.4 Native Training

Finally, we evaluate N-LSA, which is trained natively on the NTP loss alone.

Setup. We train a hybrid model of about 0.5B parameters with 24 layers, in which every fourth layer is an attention layer and the others are Gated DeltaNet layers (Yang et al., 2025b). Each attention layer has 8 query heads over a single key-value head of 128 dimensions, without positional encoding. We pre-train with a standard Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD) learning rate schedule (Hu et al., 2024), on 100B tokens of FineWeb-Edu (Penedo et al., 2024) at a context of 4k tokens in the Warmup and Stable phases, followed by 12B tokens of LongDocs in the Decay phase, at 128k tokens (Appendix C). We compare N-LSA with Full Attention, Sliding Window Attention (SWA), and the native forms of block sparse attention, NSA (Yuan et al., 2025) for Block Sparse Attention (Flat) and PISA (Tang et al., 2026) for Block Sparse Attention (Tree), all in the same model architecture and on the same data. Every sparse method attends to about 2,560 keys per query. N-LSA selects k=2048k=2048 long-range keys with flat search, next to a window of 512 keys and 4 sink keys. SWA attends to a window of 2,560 keys and 4 sink keys, NSA attends to 32 selected blocks of 64 keys and a window of 512 keys, and PISA attends to 40 blocks of 64 keys, which always include the first block and the two most recent blocks (window). We train N-LSA with flat search only, and leave native training with tree search to future work.

Figure 7 shows that N-LSA reaches the validation loss of Full Attention throughout the decay phase at 128k token context, at 1.085 against 1.085, while PISA, NSA and SWA trail at 1.100, 1.117 and 1.154. During pre-training at 4k tokens, all methods stay within 0.004 of each other, as their keys cover most of the context. Table 4 confirms this on downstream tasks. On commonsense reasoning (Clark et al., 2018; Zellers et al., 2019), all models are on par. On recall (Arora et al., 2024), N-LSA stays close to Full Attention and ahead of the other sparse methods. On RULER, N-LSA stays within 3.5 points of Full Attention up to 128k tokens, at 32.2 against 34.7 at 128k tokens, while NSA and PISA fall to 19.2 and 14.6, and SWA to 3.0 once the context outgrows its window.

N-LSA also trains faster than Full Attention at long context. For one attention layer on a single GPU, the forward and backward pass of N-LSA is 1.1×\times faster than Full Attention with FlashAttention-3 (Shah et al., 2024) at 64k tokens and 1.6×\times faster at 128k tokens (Figure 7, left). End to end, the whole model completes its decay phase 1.24×\times faster at the same validation loss (Figure 7, right), as only every fourth layer is an attention layer. At shorter contexts, the selection of the keys costs more than it saves. Its peak memory is higher, at 6.8 GiB against 5.8 GiB per layer at 128k tokens, partly because N-LSA keeps the indices of the selected keys of every query for the backward pass, which grow linearly with the context.

Overall, N-LSA trains natively at the accuracy of Full Attention and becomes faster as the context grows.

5 Discussion

LSA reduces the cost of finding the keys, but not of storing them, and the KV cache still grows linearly with the context. It is orthogonal to methods that compress the KV cache (DeepSeek-AI, 2026a), share the index across layers (Bai et al., 2026; DeepSeek-AI, 2026b), or predict several tokens per step (Gloeckle et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2024), and could be combined with each.

We observed tree search to lose accuracy faster than flat search past 1M tokens on GLM-5.3-Flash, while it overtakes flat search in decode only from about 5M tokens with one request, and is predicted to do so in prefill only beyond 10M tokens. It remains open whether sparse training would close this gap beyond indexer distillation.

We train N-LSA at a small scale, with about 0.5B parameters, up to 128k tokens and with flat search only. Scaling native training to larger models, longer contexts and tree search remains open.

6 Conclusion

At ultra-long context, the cost of sparse attention lies in finding which keys to attend to. We introduce LSA, which clusters the keys in a learned latent space and replaces the scan of every key with a search over the clusters, flat or along a tree. D-LSA distils LSA into pre-trained models and stays close to the accuracy of their baseline attention up to 10M tokens. At 10M tokens, one attention layer of D-LSA prefills 22.7×\times and decodes 4.6×\times faster than sparse attention in GLM-5.3-Flash, and 72.4×\times and 42.5×\times faster than Full Attention in Qwen-3.8-27B. End to end, this reduces the time to first token by 2.2×\times and 9.2×\times, respectively. N-LSA trains LSA natively on the next-token loss alone, at the accuracy of Full Attention and 1.6×\times faster per layer at 128k tokens. With tree search, the cost of finding the keys grows subquadratically, which makes LSA a step towards attention that scales well beyond 10M tokens. LSA thus provides a practical way forward for ultra-long context attention, both for distilling pre-trained models and for native training.

Appendix A Attention Sparsity

To test how many keys a query needs to keep accuracy, we let each query of Qwen-3.8-27B attend only to the sink, the window and its true top-kk keys (Figure 8). At 128k tokens, Top-kk Oracle Attention keeps 98% of the RULER accuracy of Full Attention down to k=512k=512, while each query attends to 0.8% of the keys. Single-needle retrieval holds down to k=16k=16, while MultiKey 2, MultiKey 3 and CWE fall first in accuracy. Therefore, sparse attention loses little if it finds the most relevant keys, which is what LSA is designed to do without scoring every key.
