Table 5 lists the symbols of LSA. Algorithm 1 clusters one cluster block into buckets, and Algorithm 2 is the beam search of D-LSA (Tree).

Appendix C Training Data

In this section, we report additional details on the training dataset we use to train D-LSA under indexer distillation, and also train N-LSA in the decay phase: LongDocs.

We use the following terminology:

  • •

    Source: a collection of documents, such as Project Gutenberg.

  • •

    Domain: a group of sources: books, academic, code, agentic, government, parliament and discussion.

  • •

    Document: one item of a source, such as a book, a paper, a code repository or an agent trace.

  • •

    Sequence: a contiguous part of one document, at a particular sequence length from 16k to 1M tokens.

Sources. LongDocs is a collection of long documents from publicly available sources and in-house agent traces. Eight sources are publicly available: Project Gutenberg, DOAB, arXiv, USGPO, UK Hansard and Wikimedia from the filtered releases of the Common Pile (Kandpal et al., 2025), The Stack (Kocetkov et al., 2023), of which we take the Python and Java repositories, and the software engineering traces of Open-SWE-Traces (NVIDIA, 2026e). The in-house agent traces are long sessions of agents that play games or solve long-context tasks, and they make up 13.1% of the training tokens. We use every public source as released.

Sequences. Each sequence comes from one document and never joins two documents. A code document is one repository, its files joined in the order of their paths, and an agent trace is one session rendered as text. We hold out 2% of the documents for validation.

Distillation training. We distil every indexer on a mix of 352M tokens drawn from LongDocs (Figure 9). The mix is uniformly sampled across domain and sequence length, with a bias towards longer context windows at 512k and 1M. In particular, we give each sequence length 32M tokens, and twice and four times as many to 512k and 1M. Sequences of 1M tokens thus hold about a third of the training tokens. We experimentally determine this choice to be beneficial, with +0.036 accuracy on RULER at 1M (averaged over 3 seeds, notable lifts in multikey_2, multikey_3, +0.35 and +0.15 respectively), while accuracy from 4k to 512k stays roughly identical. Within each length, every domain receives an equal share of the tokens. A domain with too few documents of that length gives its share to the others (parliament stops at 256k tokens and discussion at 512k).

Native training. The decay training stage of N-LSA reads the whole collection rather than the mix, without the long-context agent sessions. The data is tokenised (18.9B tokens over 134,740 documents), and cut into sequence lengths the training requires.

Appendix D PaperTrail

As part of this work, we introduce PaperTrail, an extension of the RULER (Hsieh et al., 2024) benchmark that tests models at ultra-long context in a more realistic setting, inspired by real-life scientific literature review (Figure 10). Instead of finding a needle in synthetic text, a model finds facts spread across real scientific papers and connects them, as in a literature search. We use the following terminology:

  • •

    Sample: a collection of real arXiv preprints of 2026 from one domain.

  • •

    Trail: a chain of papers that introduces a result, cites it, and later revises and renames it.

  • •

    Fabricated paper: a paper we write for a trail.

  • •

    Host paper: a real paper into which we insert passages that cite or use facts from a fabricated paper.

  • •

    Insertion: a passage we add to a host paper, which only adds sentences and never changes the text of the authors.

  • •

    Background paper: any other paper of a sample, real and unchanged.

Context. PaperTrail has three samples, on exoplanets, long-context machine learning and quantum error correction, with 1,246 papers in total. Each sample hides two trails (Trail A and Trail B). A trail has two fabricated papers and 8 to 9 insertions in 6 to 7 host papers, and background papers fill the rest of the context. An insertion places its references where an author would place them, such that a host paper reads naturally as before. Papers in the context are not presented in chronological order, and a host often comes before the paper it cites.

Trails. The first fabricated paper of a trail introduces a result, for example AlloKV, a KV cache eviction method whose budget grows as the 0.43 power of the context length. Host papers cite and use it. Two to three weeks later, the second fabricated paper revises the value and renames the method, here to SuBA with an exponent of 0.61. Host papers posted after the revision either cite the new name or still quote the old value, as real literature often does.

Questions. Each sample asks 30 scored questions, 10 per tier. A tier 1 question recalls a fact from one paper, a tier 2 question links two papers, and a tier 3 question links three or more papers, often the whole trail. Each sample also asks 6 questions whose answer is not in the papers, about an absent entity, a false premise or a near miss, which we report apart from the score (Table 8). The model ends its reply with the papers it used and its answer. A number counts within a relative tolerance of 2% by default, and a set of papers is scored by its F1 against the reference set.

Context sizes. We build each sample at 512k, 1M, 2M, 5M and 10M tokens, and every size holds every paper of the size below. The fabricated and host papers, at most 18 per sample, are the same at every size. The background papers grow the context from 25 to 30 papers at 512k to 386 to 465 papers at 10M, and spread the trails over the whole context. The trails are fabricated, and every paper up to 5M was posted after the release of both Qwen-3.8-27B and GLM-5.3-Flash, guaranteeing that no model has seen these papers in training. The 10M contexts hold papers posted at most six weeks before its release.

Controls. Four controls ask the same questions over parts of a sample: the question alone, the host papers without their insertions, the fabricated papers with the insertions alone, and the background papers alone. By construction, only the fabricated papers and the insertions hold the answers. We validate the controls with GLM-5.3-Flash and D-LSA (Training-Free) in Table 8.

Appendix E Accuracy

In this section, we show details of the evaluation setup, compare every method with its baseline on knowledge and reasoning, examine whether D-LSA changes the length of the reasoning, and break down the long-context results, RULER by task and PaperTrail by tier.

E.1 Evaluation Setup

Table 6 lists the setup of every benchmark. We sample Qwen-3.8-27B at temperature 1.0 with top-p 0.95, top-k 20, min-p 0 and no presence penalty, and GLM-5.3-Flash at temperature 1.0 with top-p 0.95, as their model cards recommend. On RULER, both models decode greedily with reasoning disabled. On every benchmark with reasoning, at most 4.6% of the replies reach the output cap of 163,840 tokens for any model and method.

E.2 Knowledge and Reasoning

Table 7 compares every method with the baselines on knowledge, reasoning and LongBench v2. Every score lies within the 95% confidence interval of the respective baselines.

E.3 Reasoning Length

Figure 12 compares the reasoning length of each method with the baseline of its model, question by question. For each question, we average the reasoning tokens over its repeats and divide them by those of the baseline on the same question, and each marker is the geometric mean of these ratios over the benchmark. The grey band of a benchmark is the median width of the 95% bootstrap intervals of its methods, and a marker inside it shows no measurable change. Every D-LSA design stays inside its band, except D-LSA (Tree) on GPQA-Diamond with Qwen-3.8-27B, which reasons 11% shorter.

E.4 RULER

Figure 11 shows the 13 tasks of RULER from 4k to 10M tokens, grouped into retrieval, tracing, aggregation and question answering. Single-needle retrieval stays at 95 or above for every method up to 5M tokens, except Block Sparse Attention (Tree), which falls to 88 and 71 at 1M tokens. MultiKey 2, MultiKey 3 and CWE fall to at most 5 at 10M tokens for every method, including the baselines, and bound the RULER average of every method. On Qwen-3.8-27B, D-LSA (Flat) exceeds baseline Full Attention at 10M tokens mostly on MultiQuery and HotpotQA, at 92 and 35 against 72 and 20. On GLM-5.3-Flash, D-LSA (Tree) falls to 60, 56 and 55 on MultiKey 1, MultiValue and VT at 10M tokens, against 100 for baseline sparse attention, and these three tasks account for most of its gap to D-LSA (Flat).

E.5 PaperTrail

Figure 13 shows the three tiers of PaperTrail and their average from 512k to 10M tokens. The harder the tier, the earlier it falls. Tier 3 questions fall to at most 19.0 at 10M tokens for every method on both models, while tier 1 questions stay above 90 on GLM-5.3-Flash. On Qwen-3.8-27B, D-LSA exceeds baseline Full Attention from 5M tokens on tier 1 and tier 2 questions, and D-LSA (Flat) reaches 53.3 and 32.2 against 32.2 and 22.2 at 10M tokens. On GLM-5.3-Flash, D-LSA trails baseline sparse attention mostly on tier 3 questions from 2M tokens, and D-LSA (Flat) also on tier 2 questions at 10M tokens, at 56.7 against 76.7.

Table 8 further reports the questions whose answer is not in the papers, at 512k tokens. Every D-LSA design recognises these questions within 3.7 points of the baseline of its model, at 96.3 to 100.0 against 100.0 for Qwen-3.8-27B and 96.3 for GLM-5.3-Flash.

E.6 Block Size

Figure 14 compares Block Sparse Attention (Tree) with blocks of 8, 16 and 64 keys, all selecting the same number of keys. At short context, every block size matches the baseline. As the context grows, accuracy falls earlier and further the larger the block, on both benchmarks and both models, as a larger block summarises more keys in one score and can hide a single relevant key. Even with blocks of eight keys, the size we use in the main results, the tree baseline trails D-LSA (Flat) at long context.

Appendix F Performance

We first introduce the hardware, describe the kernels of the indexer (Appendix F.1), and how D-LSA integrates with different parallelism strategies (Appendix F.2): Tensor Parallelism (TP) and Context Parallelism (CP).

Hardware. We run on NVIDIA H200 (Hopper) and B300 (Blackwell Ultra) GPUs, eight per node (NVLink domain), with the details presented in Table 9.

Precision. The KV cache, the index keys and the bucket centroids are in bf16. For the bucket centroids, which every decode step of the flat search reads in full, bf16 halves the bytes of fp32 at little cost to the selection. In an offline study on GLM-5.3-Flash, the bf16 indexer selects roughly 20 of the 4,096 long-range keys of the flat search differently from an fp32 reference, and changes the attention mass that the selected keys cover by less than 0.0001. Bucket centroids in fp8 would halve their bytes again, but would select about six times as many keys differently, so we keep them in bf16. We do not observe similar sensitivity for the node centroids, which we set to fp8 in D-LSA (Tree).

Conventions. We run prefill over chunks 𝒞\mathcal{C} of |𝒞|=32768\lvert\mathcal{C}\rvert=32768 consecutive queries, and decode over steps of one new query per request. All sizes are per layer, and per chunk in prefill or per step in decode. We run D-LSA with index keys and queries of d(idx)=64d^{(\mathrm{idx})}=64 dimensions, cluster blocks of ncluster=512n_{\mathrm{cluster}}=512 keys, buckets of n¯b=8\bar{n}_{b}=8 keys on average and at least npool=4n_{\mathrm{pool}}=4. Each query selects p=1024p=1024 buckets, so that even buckets of npooln_{\mathrm{pool}} keys hold its k=4096k=4096 long-range keys, and the expansion fills kk from about the best half of them on average. It also attends to nsink=4n_{\mathrm{sink}}=4 sink keys and a window of nw=nclustern_{w}=n_{\mathrm{cluster}} keys. On GLM-5.3-Flash, D-LSA (Flat) uses k=2048k=2048 and p=512p=512 for the queries in the first 1M positions of the context (Table 2), but for queries of a chunk at 10M tokens, the sizes above apply. Therefore, at a context of T=10×220≈10T=10\times 2^{20}\approx 10M tokens, a layer holds T/n¯b=1310720T/\bar{n}_{b}=1310720 buckets, whose centroids take 2​d(idx)​T/n¯b=1602d^{(\mathrm{idx})}T/\bar{n}_{b}=160 MiB.

F.1 Kernels

We refer to the steps of D-LSA by their badges in Figure 3, and Figure 15 shows how we implement each of them. We write kernels for three steps of the indexer:  clustering,  scoring and selection of the buckets, and  expansion of the selected buckets into the index lists JiJ_{i}. These kernels are written in CuTe DSL, the Python-based domain-specific language of CUTLASS (Thakkar et al., 2023), to target H200 and B300 specifically. We also keep a Triton (Tillet et al., 2019) version of each kernel, which is not tied to these two GPUs. We give the shapes and times of the kernels on H200, and note where B300 differs. For  attention, we rely on pre-existing attention kernels, that attend over the index lists JiJ_{i} unchanged. The only exception is CP (Appendix F.2), for which we do add an attention kernel.

Clustering. The clustering does relatively little work: one Gram matrix per cluster block, over its pooled keys, takes about 0.13 Gflop for a whole chunk, against 5.5 Tflop for the bucket scan at 10M tokens. Ward’s method, however, merges buckets in rounds that run one after the other. Each of these rounds scores every pair of buckets and merges the cheapest mutual pairs (Algorithm 1, lines 5-11), until mm buckets remain. The overall runtime of the clustering step is therefore set by the latency of these rounds. Our kernel cuts the time of each round by keeping its data on chip and avoiding round trips to the host between rounds. More precisely, the kernel keeps the state of a cluster block in shared memory for all its rounds, and spreads its search for partners over a thread-block cluster of up to eight streaming multiprocessors (SMs), which exchange their results through distributed shared memory. In D-LSA (Tree), each pairing that forms the node buckets (line 16) runs all its rounds in a single launch, whose thread blocks synchronise through counters in high-bandwidth memory (HBM), so the host neither launches nor reads anything between rounds.

Selection by threshold. D-LSA scores an index query qi(idx)q_{i}^{(\mathrm{idx})} against the centroids cbc_{b} of the buckets ℬi\mathcal{B}_{i} of the cluster blocks before its own, and keeps its top-pp buckets. Over the index queries of a chunk, the scores si,b=qi(idx)⋅cbs_{i,b}=q_{i}^{(\mathrm{idx})}\cdot c_{b} form a matrix with one row per query, so we call the scores of query ii its row, in decode as well. The row holds Ni=|ℬi|N_{i}=\lvert\mathcal{B}_{i}\rvert scores, which grows with the position of the query, to about T/n¯bT/\bar{n}_{b} at the end of a context of TT tokens. In prefill and in decode alike, many thread blocks compute the scores of a row, each over its own span of the row, so no thread block sees the whole row, and the selection cannot take its top-pp directly. Instead, inspired by Floyd & Rivest (1975) (who select from only the elements between two bounds estimated from a sample), before the scan, we set a threshold θi\theta_{i} for each query, and a thread block compares each of its scores with θi\theta_{i}. Then, it appends only the buckets whose score is at or above it to the list LiL_{i} of the query: one comparison per score, without seeing the rest of the row. Only the buckets of LiL_{i}, a small multiple γ​p\gamma p of them (see below), are then ranked.

We also evaluate an alternative inspired by the k-selection of FAISS (Johnson et al., 2021), which keeps the top-pp buckets of each span and merges them. With this design, every thread block has to rank its span, rather than compare each score once. Furthermore, the merge receives pp buckets from every span, rather than about γ​p\gamma p in all. Overall, at 10M tokens in prefill, a row is split into 320 spans, which list 327,680 buckets, against about 1,536 in LiL_{i}.

We aim for about γ​p\gamma p buckets of the row to score at or above θi\theta_{i}, with γ>1\gamma>1: enough to hold the top-pp with room for error, and few enough to keep LiL_{i} short. A first pass, the threshold estimate, sets θi\theta_{i} from a sample of nsn_{s} buckets of the row (Figure 16):

θi\displaystyle\theta_{i} ≤the nθ-th best sampled ​si,b\displaystyle\leq\text{the $n_{\theta}$-th best sampled }s_{i,b} (4)
≈the γ​p-th best ​si,b​ of the row\displaystyle\approx\text{the $\gamma p$-th best }s_{i,b}\text{ of the row}
nθ\displaystyle n_{\theta} =γ⋅p⋅ns/Ni\displaystyle=\gamma\cdot p\cdot n_{s}/N_{i}

The sample takes about one bucket in every Ni/nsN_{i}/n_{s} of the row, so its nθn_{\theta}-th best score ranks about nθ​Ni/ns=γ​pn_{\theta}N_{i}/n_{s}=\gamma p-th in the row, and θi\theta_{i} is placed at or just below it. This estimate is noisy: for independent samples, the count of buckets above θi\theta_{i} would typically differ from γ​p\gamma p by about γ​p/nθ\gamma p/\sqrt{n_{\theta}}. However, since neighbouring buckets are correlated, this is only a heuristic. Prefill fixes nθn_{\theta}, so that its sample grows with the row, and decode fixes nsn_{s}, and derives nθn_{\theta} for each request.

The noise affects only the cost of the selection. The threshold sets how many buckets are listed, but not which are selected: when LiL_{i} holds every bucket with si,b≥θis_{i,b}\geq\theta_{i}, and at least pp of them, the top-pp buckets of the row all reach θi\theta_{i}, and are thus all in LiL_{i}. The estimate misses in two ways: θi\theta_{i} comes out too high, and fewer than pp buckets score at or above it, or too low, and more score at or above it than LiL_{i} has room for. γ\gamma leaves room for the noise on both sides, γ​p−p\gamma p-p below and the rest of LiL_{i} above. A query that the estimate misses anyway falls back to its whole row. In prefill, it scores all its buckets again and takes their top-pp, the work the threshold avoids, but for one query rather than a whole chunk. In decode, it takes the top-pp of the scores the scan wrote. The fallback thus costs little as long as few queries take it.

Each bucket of LiL_{i} is packed with its score into one 64-bit integer σi,b\sigma_{i,b}: the bits of si,bs_{i,b}, in a form that keeps their order, in its upper 32 bits, and the bucket id, inverted, in its lower 32. A larger σi,b\sigma_{i,b} is thus a better score, or, at equal scores, a lower bucket id. The  expansion finds, by radix select (Alabi et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2023a) over the σi,b\sigma_{i,b}, the cut σi⋆\sigma_{i}^{\star} at which the buckets of LiL_{i}, taken best first, reach kk keys or pp buckets. It writes into JiJ_{i} the keys of the buckets above σi⋆\sigma_{i}^{\star}, in the order of LiL_{i}, then the first keys of the bucket at σi⋆\sigma_{i}^{\star} until JiJ_{i} holds kk. If these buckets hold fewer than kk keys outside the sink and the window, JiJ_{i} holds fewer. These are the keys that an expansion of the buckets best first would select, in another order. The attention does not depend on the order, so LiL_{i} is never sorted. Prefill and decode differ in where the scores go, how θi\theta_{i} is set, and what a fallback costs.

Flat prefill. In prefill, the flat search selects the buckets of all the queries of a chunk at once, in one matrix product on tensor cores, whose kernel compares each score with θi\theta_{i} as soon as the score is computed, without writing it to memory. We first show why the scores are not written, then how the product is spread over the GPU, and then the steps of Algorithm 3.

With the |𝒞|\lvert\mathcal{C}\rvert index queries of a chunk 𝒞\mathcal{C} as the rows of Q𝒞(idx)Q_{\mathcal{C}}^{(\mathrm{idx})}, and the T/n¯bT/\bar{n}_{b} bucket centroids cbc_{b} as the rows of CC, the rows of the chunk form one score matrix

S=Q𝒞(idx)​C⊤,Si,b=qi(idx)⋅cbS=Q_{\mathcal{C}}^{(\mathrm{idx})}C^{\top},\qquad S_{i,b}=q_{i}^{(\mathrm{idx})}\cdot c_{b} (5)

At 10M tokens, computing SS takes FpreF^{\mathrm{pre}} floating-point operations (flop) on at least BreadpreB_{\mathrm{read}}^{\mathrm{pre}} bytes of bf16 queries and centroids, and writing it takes BscorespreB_{\mathrm{scores}}^{\mathrm{pre}} bytes in fp32:

Fpre\displaystyle F^{\mathrm{pre}} =2​|𝒞|​d(idx)​T/n¯b≈5.5​Tflop\displaystyle=2\lvert\mathcal{C}\rvert\,d^{(\mathrm{idx})}\,T/\bar{n}_{b}\approx 5.5\,\text{Tflop} (6)
Breadpre\displaystyle B_{\mathrm{read}}^{\mathrm{pre}} =2​d(idx)​(T/n¯b+|𝒞|)≈164​MiB\displaystyle=2d^{(\mathrm{idx})}\big(T/\bar{n}_{b}+\lvert\mathcal{C}\rvert\big)\approx 164\,\text{MiB}
Bscorespre\displaystyle B_{\mathrm{scores}}^{\mathrm{pre}} =4​|𝒞|​T/n¯b=160​GiB\displaystyle=4\lvert\mathcal{C}\rvert\,T/\bar{n}_{b}=160\,\text{GiB}

On an H200, at the peak of its tensor cores, computing SS would take at least Fpre/989​Tflop/s=5.6F^{\mathrm{pre}}/989\,\text{Tflop/s}=5.6 ms. If every query and centroid were read from HBM only once, the products would have an arithmetic intensity of Fpre/Breadpre≈32000F^{\mathrm{pre}}/B_{\mathrm{read}}^{\mathrm{pre}}\approx 32000 flop/B, two orders of magnitude above the ridge point of the H200. Under this ideal reuse, they can be bound by compute.

Writing SS, however, is bound by memory, and would take at least Bscorespre/4.8​TB/s=36B_{\mathrm{scores}}^{\mathrm{pre}}/4.8\,\text{TB/s}=36 ms. Both are lower bounds from the peaks of the GPU, and the second is more than six times the first at any context, as both grow with TT. At 9M tokens, SS alone would already exceed the 141 GB of HBM of an H200. At long context, we therefore never write SS, and the selection writes only the lists LiL_{i}.

As in a matrix multiplication (GEMM), the product is tiled (Figure 17). A thread block holds a tile of tq=128t_{q}=128 index queries in shared memory, and streams the centroids through it in tiles of tb=64t_{b}=64 (128 on B300). It computes one tq×tbt_{q}\times t_{b} tile StileS^{\mathrm{tile}} of SS at a time, on tensor cores, and keeps it on chip. Each thread block takes such a tile of queries and a span of up to 64 tiles of centroids. At 10M tokens, a row is thus split into 320 spans, and the chunk into 256×320=81920256\times 320=81920 thread blocks, while an H200 runs 528 at a time, 4 on each of its 132 SMs, which is enough to keep every SM busy. At shorter contexts, the spans shrink, so that there are still enough thread blocks.

The bucket scan differs from a GEMM only in its epilogue. Instead of writing each entry Si,bS_{i,b} of StileS^{\mathrm{tile}}, the epilogue compares it with the threshold (lines 6-7), and compacts the buckets at or above it in shared memory, so that each span appends them to LiL_{i} in HBM with one atomic per query (line 9). With d(idx)=64d^{(\mathrm{idx})}=64, a tile takes few products, and this epilogue costs about as much as they do, so the two must overlap. On H200, the thread block splits its warps by role: one warp loads the tiles of centroids into shared memory with the Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA), in a pipeline of two stages, while a warpgroup multiplies them on tensor cores (WGMMA) into two accumulators in registers, and compares one with the threshold while the tensor cores fill the other. On B300, the products accumulate in the tensor memory of the SM instead, from which the comparing threads load them. Triton emits the same instructions, but chooses this schedule itself and gives no control of shared memory, which is why we write the scan in CuTe DSL.

At short context, below 32,768 buckets (about 256k tokens), the selection costs more than writing SS, which then takes at most 4 GiB, and we instead write SS with one matrix product in PyTorch and take the top-pp buckets of each row.

In prefill, we fix nθ=64n_{\theta}=64, so that the count above θi\theta_{i} is off by about γ​p/8\gamma p/8, and γ=1.5\gamma=1.5, which sets the sample: every (γ⋅p/nθ)=24(\gamma\cdot p/n_{\theta})=24th bucket of the row, about 4% of its scores at any context. Algorithm 3 then selects in four steps. The threshold estimate scores the sample twice on tensor cores, once for the mean and the best of its scores and once to count them in 64 bins between the two, binning them straight from the accumulators so that the scores of the sample are never written, and sets θi\theta_{i} to the lower edge of the highest bin with at least nθn_{\theta} samples at or above it (lines 1-2). The bucket scan computes SS tile by tile, and lists the buckets whose score Si,bS_{i,b} is at or above θi\theta_{i} minus a margin δ\delta (lines 3-9):

Li={b∈ℬi:Si,b≥θi−δ}L_{i}=\{\,b\in\mathcal{B}_{i}:S_{i,b}\geq\theta_{i}-\delta\,\} (7)

Candidate scoring then re-scores the buckets of LiL_{i}, as vector search re-scores a shortlist (Jégou et al., 2011): it computes their score si,bs_{i,b} again in fp32, one dot product per bucket, and packs it into σi,b\sigma_{i,b} (lines 10-11).

The margin is there because the scan and candidate scoring, which multiply the same bf16 operands and both accumulate in fp32, accumulate in different orders, so Si,bS_{i,b} and si,bs_{i,b} can differ: with unit-norm index queries and centroids and d(idx)=64d^{(\mathrm{idx})}=64, by less than 10−510^{-5}. The margin δ=10−4\delta=10^{-4} is ten times larger, so LiL_{i} holds every bucket with si,b≥θis_{i,b}\geq\theta_{i}. The list LiL_{i} has room for 3​p=30723p=3072 buckets, twice the target γ​p\gamma p. A query whose list overflows, or holds fewer than pp buckets at or above θi\theta_{i}, falls back: it scores all its buckets again, and takes their top-pp (line 12). The expansion writes JiJ_{i} (lines 13-16).

CUDA graphs. A prefill chunk takes milliseconds, against which the launches of its kernels from the host cost little, and its selection reads the sizes of its lists back on the host, so we serve prefill without graphs. A decode step of the selection, however, takes only tens of microseconds, about as long as its launches, so SGLang captures each decode step, our kernels included, in a CUDA graph, and replays it with one launch from the host. A CUDA graph fixes the shapes of its kernels, so a graph sized for the longest context the server admits would launch the thread blocks of 10M tokens at every step, whatever the contexts of the batch. We therefore capture one graph per range of context lengths, up to 1.125⋅2e1.125\cdot 2^{e} tokens for e=17,…,23e=17,\ldots,23 (from 144k to 9M), and one graph for the longest context, and each step replays the narrowest graph that covers the longest request of the batch. The threshold estimate of the flat search samples across the width of the graph, so a request far shorter than its range would see too few samples and fall back to its full row. The factor 1.125 avoids this for the common case: a request of a power-of-two length, with its answer, sits at about 89% of its range. The clustering of a complete cluster block runs outside the graph, before the replay, once every ncluster=512n_{\mathrm{cluster}}=512 decoded tokens, and the decode times of Section 4.3 spread its cost over those tokens.

Flat decode. In decode, each request adds one new query per step, whose buckets the flat search selects. It does so in a single pass, which reads the centroids of the request once, scores them, and lists LiL_{i} as it goes. We first show why this one read sets its time, then how the pass is spread over the GPU, and then the steps of Algorithm 4.

In decode, SS is a single row: the one index query qi(idx)q_{i}^{(\mathrm{idx})} of a request scores each of its T/n¯bT/\bar{n}_{b} centroids cbc_{b} once per step. With |𝒞|=1\lvert\mathcal{C}\rvert=1 in Equation 6, a step at 10M tokens takes FdecF^{\mathrm{dec}} flop on at least BreaddecB_{\mathrm{read}}^{\mathrm{dec}} bytes, and writing its row takes BscoresdecB_{\mathrm{scores}}^{\mathrm{dec}} bytes in fp32:

Fdec\displaystyle F^{\mathrm{dec}} =2​d(idx)​T/n¯b≈168​Mflop\displaystyle=2d^{(\mathrm{idx})}\,T/\bar{n}_{b}\approx 168\,\text{Mflop} (8)
Breaddec\displaystyle B_{\mathrm{read}}^{\mathrm{dec}} =2​d(idx)​(T/n¯b+1)≈160​MiB\displaystyle=2d^{(\mathrm{idx})}\big(T/\bar{n}_{b}+1\big)\approx 160\,\text{MiB}
Bscoresdec\displaystyle B_{\mathrm{scores}}^{\mathrm{dec}} =4​T/n¯b=5​MiB\displaystyle=4\,T/\bar{n}_{b}=5\,\text{MiB}

Its arithmetic intensity Fdec/Breaddec≈1F^{\mathrm{dec}}/B_{\mathrm{read}}^{\mathrm{dec}}\approx 1 flop/B is far below the ridge point: the selection is bound by memory, and reading the centroids once would take at least Breaddec/4.8​TB/s=35B_{\mathrm{read}}^{\mathrm{dec}}/4.8\,\text{TB/s}=35 µs on H200. Prefill, bound by compute, can afford to read the centroids more than once: every tile of queries reads them all, and candidate scoring reads those of LiL_{i} again. In decode, a second read would about double the bytes the scan reads, so Algorithm 4 selects within a single read of the centroids, besides the small sample of its threshold estimate. It can, however, afford to write every si,bs_{i,b} to HBM, which adds only 3% to the bytes it moves, so that its fallback takes the top-pp of the written scores, without reading the centroids again. The threshold is thus not strictly needed in decode, but it saves a selection over all NiN_{i} written scores of each request: the expansion ranks only the buckets of LiL_{i}.

With a single query, only the row is split: the scan takes spans of 256 buckets, one per thread block. The centroids of a request lie in pages of Bcache(idx)B_{\mathrm{cache}}^{(\mathrm{idx})}, as its keys lie in pages of the KV cache, and each thread block reads the cbc_{b} of its span through the page table of the request. The threshold estimate and the scan score on the CUDA cores, with the same dot product: at 1 flop/B the scan is bound by HBM, not by arithmetic, and gains nothing from tensor cores. A request whose row fits in its list takes every bucket.

Each CUDA graph samples a fixed number nsn_{s} of buckets, from 2,048 to 16,384, in runs of 8 neighbouring buckets of a page, spread evenly over the row. A graph that covers longer contexts thus samples a smaller share of the row, with a smaller nθn_{\theta} and a noisier estimate, so the target γ​p\gamma p grows with the graph, from 1.5​p1.5p to 3​p3p. We set γ\gamma for each graph by hand, so that LiL_{i} still holds at least pp buckets, and fits in its buffer, when the count misses γ​p\gamma p by four times the deviation above, 4​γ​p/nθ4\gamma p/\sqrt{n_{\theta}}. Algorithm 4 runs in four launches, followed by the expansion, and has no candidate scoring. The threshold estimate takes two launches: one scores the sample, and one finds its nθn_{\theta}-th best score by radix select over the bits of the scores, and rounds it down (lines 1-2). The bucket scan writes the si,bs_{i,b} of each span, and appends the buckets with si,b≥θis_{i,b}\geq\theta_{i} to LiL_{i}, already packed as σi,b\sigma_{i,b} (lines 3-6). It compares the very scores that rank the buckets, so it needs no margin. The listing gathers into LiL_{i} the spans that the thread blocks appended, in bucket order (line 7), and the expansion is that of Algorithm 3 (line 9). The list LiL_{i} has room for 2,048 to 8,192 buckets, by graph, and a request whose list overflows, or holds fewer than pp buckets, falls back to the top-pp of the scores the scan wrote (line 8). Programmatic dependent launch (NVIDIA, 2026f), a feature of Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, lets a kernel start while the one before it still runs, and wait for its results only where it reads them (line 5). The scan thus reads and scores the centroids while θi\theta_{i} is still being computed.

Tree prefill. In prefill, the beam search (Algorithm 2) starts at the lowest level with at most nstart=32768n_{\mathrm{start}}=32768 node buckets, a value we chose by a sweep of accuracy against time. It keeps a beam of pℓ=2048p_{\ell}=2048 node buckets on every level. The descent starts from every node bucket of this level (line 1), which one matrix product in cuBLAS scores in full. Each level of the descent (lines 2-7) then runs in one kernel (five or six launches in Triton), besides a matrix product in cuBLAS that scores the open node buckets of the level. In this kernel, a thread block holds the scores of one query in shared memory, one 32-bit word per candidate, up to the 227 KiB a thread block can take. It scores the children of the node buckets kept on the level above (line 3). It then finds the pℓp_{\ell}-th score by a radix select of four passes, each of which counts one byte of the words in a histogram of 256 bins (line 4). Finally, it writes the children of the node buckets it keeps as the candidates CC of the next level (line 5). Above about 24k node buckets, keeping the beam of the start level this way would leave a single thread block per SM, so it takes two launches instead: a listing of the node buckets above a sampled threshold, as in the flat search, and the keep of the beam. At level 0 (lines 8-9), the thread block writes the top-pp buckets as packed scores σi,b\sigma_{i,b}. The expansion of Algorithm 3 (lines 13-16) reads them as it reads LiL_{i}.

Tree decode. In decode, the new queries of all the requests of a batch descend together, through the beam kernels of the prefill, but over a copy of the hierarchy at fixed addresses, and at shapes set by the longest context, so that a CUDA graph can replay the step. Each request adds one query per step, but the descent still runs its levels one after another, so its time barely changes with the number of requests, while the flat search scans every bucket once per request. Every query scores the levels from the top level of the longest context down, and holds no candidates above its own start level. A step takes 7 to 13 kernels from 128k to 10M tokens, as the number of levels grows with the context.

Other steps. The remaining steps of D-LSA are the projections and the L2 normalisation of the index keys kj(idx)k_{j}^{(\mathrm{idx})} and queries qi(idx)q_{i}^{(\mathrm{idx})}, the pooling, and the tables of Bcache(idx)B_{\mathrm{cache}}^{(\mathrm{idx})}. They consist of matrix products, reductions and a sort, which run as standard PyTorch operations, with the products through cuBLAS. These steps cost little next to the scoring. On GLM-5.3-Flash, for example, each of the two projections of a chunk of 32,768 tokens from the 512 dimensions of the latent takes 2⋅32768⋅512⋅642\cdot 32768\cdot 512\cdot 64 flop, 4.3 Gflop for both. This is under 1% of the scoring of the chunk at contexts of 1M tokens and beyond (Equation 6).

Attention kernels. D-LSA attends through existing kernels, which only need to read the index lists in a layout of their own. The expansion writes the index list JiJ_{i} of every query ii as a row of nsink+k+nw=4612n_{\mathrm{sink}}+k+n_{w}=4612 int32 entries. Each entry is the slot in the KV cache of one key j∈Jij\in J_{i}, and the row is padded with −1-1 when the query has fewer keys to attend to. The index lists of a chunk 𝒞\mathcal{C} thus form one matrix of |𝒞|\lvert\mathcal{C}\rvert rows. On GLM-5.3-Flash, JiJ_{i} takes the place of the index list of the model’s own indexer, and the sparse attention of SGLang attends over it unchanged. On Qwen-3.8-27B, we pass every query ii to a paged attention kernel as a sequence of its own: its row is the page table, each page holds one slot, and the sequence length is |Ji|\lvert J_{i}\rvert. Table 10 lists the attention kernels we use, from FlashAttention-3 (FA3) (Shah et al., 2024) and its successor FA4, FlashMLA (Li et al., 2025), the TRT-LLM kernels of FlashInfer (Ye et al., 2025) and Triton. Each is the default of SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024) for its model and GPU, except where that default cannot run. For instance, on B300, D-LSA on Qwen-3.8-27B attends through the Triton kernel of SGLang, as FlashAttention supports pages of a single slot only on Hopper. With CP8, GLM-5.3-Flash decodes through a split-KV sparse kernel that we add to SGLang (Appendix F.2), and on B300 it prefills through a TileLang kernel (Wang et al., 2025). With decode context parallelism (DCP8, Appendix F.2) on H200, Full Attention and Block Sparse Attention (Flat) on Qwen-3.8-27B decode through Triton kernels.

N-LSA training. The kernels above serve D-LSA at inference. N-LSA also needs kernels for training, for its forward and its backward pass, with which a layer is up to 1.6×\times faster than with Full Attention at 128k tokens (Section 4.4).

A few changes stem from the architectural differences of N-LSA compared to D-LSA. A training step processes whole sequences, of up to 128k tokens in our runs, with no KV cache and no decode, so every query of a sequence selects at once, as in a prefill chunk as long as the sequence. The keys change at every step as the attention projections learn, so every step clusters all keys again, where D-LSA clusters each cluster block once and keeps its buckets in the cache. The selection clusters and scores the attention’s own normalised keys and queries, of dimension 128, and takes the best score of the 8 query heads (Equation 3). At 128k tokens, a row holds at most 16,384 buckets, from which a query selects p=512p=512 for k=2048k=2048 keys, next to a window of 512 keys and 4 sink keys. Finally, every step runs a backward pass, which D-LSA never does at long context.

Two of these differences shape the kernels. As the rows are short, the selection places θi\theta_{i} from the whole row rather than from a sample: a first pass over the row counts its scores in a histogram of 256 bins, and a second lists the buckets from the bin of the pp-th score up, both on tensor cores, and the top-pp of the list are then taken by their scores. The backward pass is the main addition. As N-LSA stops the gradient through the selection, the clustering and the scoring of the centroids need no backward pass, and the only new backward kernel is that of the sparse attention. For one query head, with logits zi,j=qi⋅kj/dhz_{i,j}=q_{i}\cdot k_{j}/\sqrt{d_{h}}, its forward pass, as in any attention kernel, runs over the queries, each query ii attending to the keys it selected and writing only its own output:

oi=∑j∈Jiαi,j​vj,αi,j=softmaxj∈Ji​(zi,j)o_{i}=\sum_{j\in J_{i}}\alpha_{i,j}v_{j},\qquad\alpha_{i,j}=\mathrm{softmax}_{j\in J_{i}}\left(z_{i,j}\right) (9)

Its backward pass cannot run over the queries in the same way, as each key jj and its value receive a gradient of the NTP loss ℒ\mathcal{L} from every query that selected the key:

∂ℒ∂kj=∑i∈Ij∂ℒ∂zi,j​qidh,∂ℒ∂vj=∑i∈Ijαi,j​∂ℒ∂oi\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial k_{j}}=\sum_{i\in I_{j}}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial z_{i,j}}\frac{q_{i}}{\sqrt{d_{h}}},\qquad\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial v_{j}}=\sum_{i\in I_{j}}\alpha_{i,j}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial o_{i}} (10)

where Ij={i:j∈Ji}I_{j}=\{\,i:j\in J_{i}\,\}, and the queries of IjI_{j} lie anywhere in the sequence at or after jj. As the 8 query heads share one key-value head, ∂ℒ/∂kj\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial k_{j} and ∂ℒ/∂vj\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial v_{j} also sum over the heads. Run over the queries, the backward pass would have many thread blocks add into the gradient of the same key, with an atomic addition for each share. The backward kernels instead run over the keys, as the backward pass of FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022) does for dense attention (Algorithm 5). With a sparse selection, this first requires inverting the selection, listing the queries of each group of keys (lines 1-2). A thread block then holds the gradients of a group of keys in registers, adds the shares of these queries into them (lines 4-9), and writes them with few atomic additions (line 11). The gradient of each query sums over its own JiJ_{i}, so a separate pass gathers it as in the forward pass, computing ∂ℒ/∂zi,j\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial z_{i,j} again (line 12). To invert it, the backward pass needs the selection of every query, the kk int32 long-range indices that the forward pass keeps, as the sink and the window follow from the positions: 1 GiB at 128k tokens, about the gap between the peak memory of N-LSA and that of Full Attention. Evaluating and implementing a port of these kernels to CuTe DSL, as for D-LSA, is left to future work.

With these kernels, Section 4.4 times one attention layer of N-LSA on one H200, at batch 1 in bf16, against the same layer with causal attention in FA3. Each time covers the forward and the backward pass of the whole layer, from its input projections to its output projection, with the clustering and the selection.

Measurements. Table 11 times each step on one H200 with Nsight Compute, in a single profile with the clocks unlocked, with its CuTe DSL and its Triton kernels. The inputs are synthetic, at the shapes we serve: a prefill chunk of 32,768 queries at 10M tokens, a beam of pℓ=2048p_{\ell}=2048 over node buckets of nb,ℓ=4n_{b,\ell}=4, decode with one request at 10M tokens, the Ward clustering of the 64 cluster blocks of one prefill chunk, and the clustering of one node block of ncluster,ℓ=4096n_{\mathrm{cluster},\ell}=4096 buckets into node buckets. The times are those of the kernels alone, without the PyTorch launches between them. The regime of a step is where its main CuTe DSL kernel sits: bound by compute or by memory, with its share of the bf16 peak or of the HBM bandwidth of Table 9, bound by neither as a radix select over packed integer keys (selection), or limited by its serial rounds (latency). The bucket scan, the largest step of the flat prefill, reaches 49% of the bf16 peak and uses 1% of the HBM bandwidth, so the tiles of queries reread the centroids mostly from the L2 cache. On real inputs, the index queries of 12 held-out documents of 1M tokens and 3 books of 10M tokens on GLM-5.3-Flash, over all its sparse layers, LiL_{i} holds 1,679 buckets on average at 1M tokens and 1,737 at 10M, never overflows, and falls back, with fewer than pp buckets above θi\theta_{i}, for 5×10−55\times 10^{-5} of the queries at 1M and 10−310^{-3} at 10M. In decode, 3×10−43\times 10^{-4} of the steps fall back at 1M, mostly as their lists overflow, and none at 10M. The decode scan reads at 3.58 TB/s, 75% of the HBM bandwidth. At 10M tokens, the CuTe DSL kernels are faster than the Triton ones in every step, from 1.02×\times for candidate scoring, which is bound by the HBM bandwidth in both languages, to 4.4×\times for the threshold estimate. On B300, they are faster by up to 4.3×\times in every step but level 0 of the tree search, where the two languages tie. Of the 22 ms that CuTe DSL saves on a prefill chunk at 10M tokens, 13.4 ms come from the bucket scan, mostly from overlapping its epilogue with its products, and 6.8 ms from the threshold estimate, whose Triton version writes the scores of its sample to HBM and reads them twice. The Triton versions of other steps take more launches or more passes: the node-bucket clustering takes three launches per round and reads two flags on the host every eight rounds (3.4×\times), and the expansion finds its cut one bit per pass rather than one byte (1.75×\times). Table 11 sums the kernel times of the four launches of the decode select (the sample, the threshold, the scan and the listing), 71 µs at 10M tokens. Replayed from a CUDA graph, where programmatic dependent launch overlaps them, they take 14.7 µs at 1M tokens and 60.7 µs at 10M, against 36.4 µs and 146.6 µs in Triton. With the expansion and the other kernels of the selection, a flat decode step selects in 35 µs at 1M tokens and 86 µs at 10M, and Table 12 compares it with the tree search. With one request, the flat search is faster up to about 5M tokens. With 4 and 16 requests, the tree search is faster from about 1M and 256k tokens, and with 16 requests it is 5.6×\times faster at 10M tokens. As we evaluate one request at a time, every result of D-LSA (Tree) decodes with the flat search, and only its prefill uses the tree. At 1M tokens, the four steps of the flat prefill take 5.2 ms in CuTe DSL against 9.4 ms in Triton. For a whole layer of GLM-5.3-Flash on H200, CuTe DSL makes a prefill chunk at 10M tokens 1.35×\times faster than Triton.

F.2 Parallelism

We describe our integration of D-LSA with tensor (TP) and context parallelism (CP) in SGLang, for multi-head latent attention (MLA), as in GLM-5.3-Flash, and for grouped-query attention (GQA), as in Qwen-3.8-27B. NN denotes the number of ranks of a parallel group, and rr one of them. We study setups with N=8N=8 (size of our NVLink domain).

LSA is orthogonal to expert and pipeline parallelism: the former splits only the experts, and the latter keeps the index of a layer co-located with its attention on the same rank, so in this section we do not describe these two mesh configurations, but focus on TP and CP instead.

For both TP and CP, every rank holds the whole bucket cache Bcache(idx)B_{\mathrm{cache}}^{(\mathrm{idx})}, which trades memory for communication (Section 3). Table 13 summarises the communication that the indexer adds for the two mesh configurations. We discuss these in more detail below.

Tensor parallelism. We first describe TP alone, without CP, as illustrated in Figure 18. For TP, work gets split by head:  rank rr holds a set 𝒬r\mathcal{Q}_{r} of nh/Nn_{h}/N query heads, and projects them into a partial index query qi,r(idx)q_{i,r}^{(\mathrm{idx})}:

qi,r(idx)=∑h∈𝒬rqi,h(attn)​WQ(idx)q_{i,r}^{(\mathrm{idx})}=\sum_{h\in\mathcal{Q}_{r}}q_{i,h}^{(\mathrm{attn})}W_{Q}^{(\mathrm{idx})} (11)

With MLA, the ranks sum the query heads qi,h(attn)q_{i,h}^{(\mathrm{attn})} on the latent instead, and apply WQ(idx)W_{Q}^{(\mathrm{idx})} to the sum after the AllReduce below, which is equivalent by linearity.  With MLA, the latent kj(attn)k_{j}^{(\mathrm{attn})} is shared by all heads, thus replicated on every rank. With GQA, the KV heads are split across ranks too, and an index key kj(idx)k_{j}^{(\mathrm{idx})} is projected from all of them, so rank rr projects the keys kj,g(attn)k_{j,g}^{(\mathrm{attn})} of the set 𝒦r\mathcal{K}_{r} of KV heads it contributes into a partial index key kj,r(idx)k_{j,r}^{(\mathrm{idx})}:

kj,r(idx)=∑g∈𝒦rkj,g(attn)​WK,g(idx)k_{j,r}^{(\mathrm{idx})}=\sum_{g\in\mathcal{K}_{r}}k_{j,g}^{(\mathrm{attn})}W_{K,g}^{(\mathrm{idx})} (12)

where WK,g(idx)W_{K,g}^{(\mathrm{idx})} are the rows of WK(idx)W_{K}^{(\mathrm{idx})} that project KV head gg. Likewise, query head hh uses only the rows WQ,g⁡(h)(idx)W_{Q,g(h)}^{(\mathrm{idx})} of the KV head g⁡(h)g(h) it attends, in place of WQ(idx)W_{Q}^{(\mathrm{idx})} in Equation 11.

For TP8, the four KV heads of Qwen-3.8-27B are each replicated on two ranks: both contribute their own query heads, but only one counts the KV head in its 𝒦r\mathcal{K}_{r}, and the other contributes kj,r(idx)=0k_{j,r}^{(\mathrm{idx})}=0. One AllReduce sums the partials, in fp32, into the projections of Equation 1, before their normalisation:

qi(idx)=∑rqi,r(idx),kj(idx)=∑rkj,r(idx)q_{i}^{(\mathrm{idx})}=\sum_{r}q_{i,r}^{(\mathrm{idx})},\qquad k_{j}^{(\mathrm{idx})}=\sum_{r}k_{j,r}^{(\mathrm{idx})} (13)

Every rank thus holds the same index query qi(idx)q_{i}^{(\mathrm{idx})} and selects the same JiJ_{i} from its copy of Bcache(idx)B_{\mathrm{cache}}^{(\mathrm{idx})}.  It attends over JiJ_{i} with its own query heads 𝒬r\mathcal{Q}_{r}.  The clustering takes the index keys kj(idx)k_{j}^{(\mathrm{idx})} of a cluster block only once all its nclustern_{\mathrm{cluster}} keys have arrived, over several chunks or decode steps. With MLA, a rank recomputes them from the latents kj(attn)k_{j}^{(\mathrm{attn})} in its KV cache, so they are never stored. With GQA, a rank holds only some KV heads, so it cannot recompute them alone. Instead, it stores kj(idx)k_{j}^{(\mathrm{idx})} once summed: the AllReduce of Equation 13 carries the partial key kj,r(idx)k_{j,r}^{(\mathrm{idx})} of a token together with the token’s own partial query, so storing it costs memory, 2​d(idx)=1282d^{(\mathrm{idx})}=128 B per token, but no communication. Recomputing it would save that memory, at the cost of a second AllReduce of the fp32 partial keys, 256 B per token, once each block is complete.

With MLA, the AllReduce carries the 512 dimensions of the latent, 2 KiB. Since the KV cache is replicated, Bcache(idx)B_{\mathrm{cache}}^{(\mathrm{idx})} adds the same 24.5 B per token to the 1 KiB of KV cache as without parallelism.

With GQA, the AllReduce carries the partial index query and key, 512 B. A rank of Qwen-3.8-27B holds one of its four KV heads, 1 KiB, to which the indexer adds 24.5 B of bucket cache and 2​d(idx)=1282d^{(\mathrm{idx})}=128 B of stored index key.

Context parallelism. CP splits work by token in two ways (Liu et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025a), which we describe in the following, and illustrate in Figure 19.

Decode context parallelism (DCP), also called KV parallelism (Bhatia et al., 2025), splits the KV cache across the ranks, in both prefill and decode, so that each rank stores only 1/N1/N of it, which lets a context of millions of tokens fit in HBM, and reads only its share in each decode step. SGLang deals the tokens out round-robin: token jj goes to rank rjr_{j}, its slot in the KV cache modulo NN, and that rank holds key kjk_{j} and thus computes index key kj(idx)k_{j}^{(\mathrm{idx})}.

Prefill context parallelism (PCP) also splits the query rows of a chunk 𝒞\mathcal{C}, giving rank rr the rows 𝒞r\mathcal{C}_{r}, so that it selects the index lists JiJ_{i} of its own rows i∈𝒞ri\in\mathcal{C}_{r} only. The index query is not split: with PCP, every rank holds in prefill all nhn_{h} query heads qi,h(attn)q_{i,h}^{(\mathrm{attn})} of its rows, and in decode (and with GQA also in prefill), the ranks gather them, as the attention does anyway, so every rank computes qi(idx)q_{i}^{(\mathrm{idx})} itself.

We extend SGLang with PCP for GLM-5.3-Flash, which leaves us free to choose its layout, for both the base model and LSA. We make each 𝒞r\mathcal{C}_{r} one contiguous span of 𝒞\mathcal{C}, which lets the linear-attention layers pass their recurrent state along it. LSA does not depend on this split, but it is a natural fit: as every query attends a fixed budget of keys, a contiguous split already balances the sparse attention across ranks, whereas dense causal attention commonly uses a zigzag or striped split to balance its causal work (Brandon et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025a).

With MLA, we use both PCP and DCP (Figure 19, top), with no TP in the prefill attention, since SGLang was already developing PCP for GLM-5.3-Flash, while it had none for Qwen-3.8-27B. This also suits LSA: PCP splits the prefill by query rows rather than by heads.  Every rank thus holds all query heads of its rows and computes their index queries qi(idx)q_{i}^{(\mathrm{idx})}, i∈𝒞ri\in\mathcal{C}_{r}, alone, without the AllReduce of Equation 13 that TP needs. For PCP, the attention already gathers the latents K𝒞(attn)K_{\mathcal{C}}^{(\mathrm{attn})} of the whole chunk.  Every rank thus projects the index keys K𝒞(idx)K_{\mathcal{C}}^{(\mathrm{idx})} of the whole chunk itself, and  clusters them into the same Bcache(idx)B_{\mathrm{cache}}^{(\mathrm{idx})}. The indexer thus adds no communication, as long as each chunk starts on a cluster block, as chunks of 32768=64​ncluster32768=64\,n_{\mathrm{cluster}} tokens do.  Each rank selects JiJ_{i} for its rows i∈𝒞ri\in\mathcal{C}_{r}, but DCP splits the KV cache of the prefix across ranks, so most of the selected keys j∈Jij\in J_{i} live on other ranks, rj≠rr_{j}\neq r. The sparse attention, of the base model as of LSA, gathers only those rows.  Every rank marks the prefix rows that its lists JiJ_{i}, i∈𝒞ri\in\mathcal{C}_{r}, select in a mask J𝒞rJ_{\mathcal{C}_{r}} of one byte per prefix row, and one AllReduce with the maximum gives every rank their union J𝒞J_{\mathcal{C}} over the chunk, less the chunk itself, whose rows every rank already holds:

J𝒞=⋃i∈𝒞Ji∖𝒞J_{\mathcal{C}}=\bigcup_{i\in\mathcal{C}}J_{i}\setminus\mathcal{C} (14)

Each rank then contributes the latents KJ𝒞,r(attn)K_{J_{\mathcal{C}},r}^{(\mathrm{attn})} of the rows of J𝒞J_{\mathcal{C}} it holds, padded to the largest count over the ranks, to one AllGather, which gives every rank all of J𝒞J_{\mathcal{C}}. Every rank lays them out with the rows of the chunk in one buffer, KJ𝒞∪𝒞(attn)K_{J_{\mathcal{C}}\cup\mathcal{C}}^{(\mathrm{attn})}, and remaps JiJ_{i}, i∈𝒞ri\in\mathcal{C}_{r}, onto it.  The attention kernel then runs unchanged on the remapped lists. Without the mask, every rank would gather the whole prefix, 1 KiB per row, or 10 GiB per layer at a prefix of T=10T=10M tokens, while the mask costs 1 B per row. Empirically, in our runs of GLM-5.3-Flash on a 10M-token prompt, the union J𝒞J_{\mathcal{C}} of the index lists of all 32,768 queries of a late chunk covers only about 30% of the prefix, as nearby queries select largely the same keys, so the AllGather moves, and every rank holds, about 30% of the prefix rather than all of it, up to the padding.

With GQA, we run attention with TP8 and add DCP8, without PCP: TP splits the prefill by head and computes the keys of the whole chunk on every rank, and DCP splits the KV cache, which is what lets a context of 10M tokens fit on one node. DCP8 replaces the split of the KV heads: every rank holds all four KV heads of the tokens it owns, rj=rr_{j}=r, and gathers the query heads of the other ranks before the indexer and the attention, in prefill and decode. It thus needs neither the partial sums of Equation 13 nor a stored kj(idx)k_{j}^{(\mathrm{idx})}: like MLA, it recomputes the index keys of its own tokens from its KV cache.

In decode (Figure 19, bottom), each new token jj is written to its rank rjr_{j}, so the keys of a cluster block are spread across all ranks.  Once its nclustern_{\mathrm{cluster}} keys are complete, every rank needs all their index keys kj(idx)k_{j}^{(\mathrm{idx})}, but can compute only those with rj=rr_{j}=r. Each rank writes them into an ncluster×d(idx)n_{\mathrm{cluster}}\times d^{(\mathrm{idx})} buffer, one row per token of the block in order, with zeros in the rows of the other ranks, and one AllReduce sums the buffers, 64 KiB per block in bf16, or 128 B per token. As every row is non-zero on one rank only, the sum gathers the keys of the block in order, where an AllGather would group them by rank.  Every rank then clusters the same keys into the same buckets of Bcache(idx)B_{\mathrm{cache}}^{(\mathrm{idx})}. Until then, the keys of the block are covered by the window of the nwn_{w} most recent keys, which is selected by position, so they need no index key. This AllReduce runs before the CUDA graph of the decode step is replayed. In decode the attention splits the query heads across the ranks, by TP with GQA and, with MLA, by a split of the MLA heads that we add to SGLang, so every rank gathers all nhn_{h} query heads qi,h(attn)q_{i,h}^{(\mathrm{attn})} of every request, as the attention does anyway.  Every rank thus projects the same index query qi(idx)q_{i}^{(\mathrm{idx})},  selects the same JiJ_{i}, and  attends over the entries of JiJ_{i} it holds,

Ji,r={j∈Ji:rj=r}J_{i,r}=\{\,j\in J_{i}:r_{j}=r\,\} (15)

into a partial output oi,ro_{i,r}, softmax-normalised over Ji,rJ_{i,r}, with λi,r\lambda_{i,r} the log-sum-exp of its logits.  The ranks merge the partial outputs of each query head by their log-sum-exp (Dao et al., 2023):

oi=∑reλi,r−λioi,r,λi=log∑reλi,ro_{i}=\sum_{r}e^{\lambda_{i,r}-\lambda_{i}}\,o_{i,r},\qquad\lambda_{i}=\log\sum_{r}e^{\lambda_{i,r}} (16)

As the Ji,rJ_{i,r} partition JiJ_{i}, oio_{i} is the attention over JiJ_{i}, up to floating-point rounding.

Memory. Replicating Bcache(idx)B_{\mathrm{cache}}^{(\mathrm{idx})} trades memory for communication. With βKV\beta_{\mathrm{KV}} and βB\beta_{B} the bytes per token of the KV cache and of the bucket cache, the persistent storage of the KV cache and the flat index, per layer and rank, is approximately

T⁡(βKVN+βB)T\left(\frac{\beta_{\mathrm{KV}}}{N}+\beta_{B}\right) (17)

where βB≈24.5\beta_{B}\approx 24.5 B, and βKV=1024\beta_{\mathrm{KV}}=1024 B for GLM-5.3-Flash and 4,096 B for Qwen-3.8-27B. At T=10T=10M with DCP8, the bucket cache adds 246 MiB as measured, T​βBT\beta_{B} plus padding rows, to the T​βKV/N=1.25T\beta_{\mathrm{KV}}/N=1.25 GiB share of the KV cache of a layer of GLM-5.3-Flash (+19%), and 5% on Qwen-3.8-27B. An index per rank over its own keys would avoid the AllReduce of the keys, but its buckets and its JiJ_{i} would differ from those of a single GPU.
